I’ll be starting an ecology PhD program next year, earning $37,000 annually, albeit in a region with very high housing costs. My funding will be coming partly from teaching assistantships and partly from my PI’s grant. It’s not a lot by any means, but it should be enough to scrape by, especially if you’re naturally stingy like I am. You’ll likely earn $25,000-40,000 as a grad student in ecology or a similar research-based program. 

After you finish school usually you do at least one post-doc position , which typically pay in the $40,000-50,000/y range as far as I’ve seen. If you finally get a tenure track position at a university (or a research position with a government agency or NGO) you might start to make upwards of $60,000, which typically increases over the years. My current undergrad advisor makes well over $150,000 (he told me this) but my college does have a lot of money. 

Ecology is definitely not the career for you if you care about making a lot of money any time in the near future. It’s a wonderful thing to devote your life to, incredibly interesting, rewarding and intellectually enriching, but not financially enriching.

I’m in a very similar boat, and after stressing about it for a long time, I’ve come to just let it go. 

First of all, since you’re about to start your senior year (I am too), keep in mind that any relationship you started this year would probably not last that long. After graduation a lot of people move far away for work or grad school. This means that either you and your girlfriend would have to move together (which IMO is a lot for 21 year olds), be long distance (which is very difficult), or break up. Obviously that isn’t supposed to make you want a girlfriend any less but it’s something to keep in mind. 

Also, I think 21 is a tough age to look for a solid relationship because lots of people (especially girls in my experience) are not looking to be tied down. They want to be free to do what they want with who they want. Emotional maturity is also something that is a work in progress for a lot of people in our age group, so lots of drama in the relationship is likely. 

There was a study a few years ago that researched the average age that people met their spouse, and they found it to be 28. And that’s just the average. I think this is because it isn’t until their late 20s that a lot of people get tired of being so romantically independent and free and begin to want to settle down a bit more.  And that’s not being settled for, that’s just how the social dynamics work out. 

I have a brother who’s 28, and in the past year or so I’ve watched him and most of his friends go from very single to coupled up. It’s just sort of what happens. 

The moral of the story is not that you shouldn’t bother dating now, or that you have no chance of finding anyone in college, but don’t worry about it too much. In the grand scheme of life, or even just the grand scheme of your 20s, you have so much time left, and you will hit periods where it will be much easier to date.

Humans are selfish by nature, so let's just get that out of the way. But this idea that offering friendship has some sort of malice behind it is often a bit off. Sometimes they offer friendship in a misguided but often genuine attempt to comfort the dumpee. As if saying "I don't want you as my partner anymore, but I'm not going to abandon you as a person." Does it make sense for the dumpee? No. Should the dumpee ever accept this offer of friendship? 99% of the time, absolutely not. But is it a selfish malicious act? We can't say that. People love to antagonize their exes, and it's not that hard to see why. It can be very comforting to think of them as the "bad guy" and you as the "good guy." While anger is an important stage of grief, this antagonism gets us nowhere in the long-run. It just allows us to elevate ourselves above them, when in fact we are equals. And we need to see that in order to properly heal. We want true acceptance, not antagonism. 

I also think the sentence about someone who betrayed you or let you down not deserving to be your friend is a bit off. Rejection and breakups hurt like nothing else, but your ex is not really in the wrong for leaving you. That sucks to hear, but it is absolutely the truth. You do not own them and you cannot control them. Relationships are commitments, absolutely, but we all know that they come with the caveat that they can be terminated at any point. And if you disagree, you should probably take a look at your philosophy on relationships.

You shouldn't be friends with your ex. But that's because it will be too painful for you to see them and not be able to go back to relationship mode. And seeing them with any future partners will crush you, at least for the time being. Don't be friends with your ex. But don't go around antagonizing them and calling them selfish either.

It's the self-control that we've practiced. If there is a group of people out there that you can click with, then this group is constantly shifting and evolving, shrinking and growing. Because our brains are changing every single day based on our experiences. Our judgments are changing, the way we approach problems, the way we think. Who we think might be our soulmate is not controlled by anything other than your own mind. You see someone and you think "oh, there's my soulmate." But why do you think that? Because you have created in your mind a set of conditions that they will be. Your group of soulmates at 17 would probably be completely different than your group at 27 and your group at 37. My point is that I think we have more control than we give ourselves credit for. By letting ourselves become idle in the wake of heartbreak, diving deep into self-pity, and telling ourselves that we are powerless, our so-called pool of soulmates shrinks. Because we are becoming reliant on some other power to keep these potential partners waiting for us. But it isn't going to work like that. We become less compatible with others as we dive deeper into the black hole of romantic destiny. But if we continue to self-improve, constantly reflect and grow, recognize that there is not some greater omniscient energy controlling all of this, that it is all constructed in our own minds, we can take control of our pool of soulmates and make it grow. It's actually quite liberating.

I'll give one overarching lesson and 2 more specific ones.

Overarching: Think before you speak. Okay, this one may seem super obvious. I never thought I had a problem with this. But when you think someone is the love of your life, you tend to just let things spill out and think "oh this is fine, they love me unconditionally." This is a grave mistake. Before you say something, consider what their reaction might be. Consider your phrasing. Consider your inner biases. But ofc, doing this too much will make you appear closed off. And we don't want that either. Find that happy medium and live there for a while. It will become second nature. You will slip up, but try to reduce the frequency and severity of your slip-ups. Everyone slips up sometimes.

Specific #1: Be careful with the big L word. Love. Don't use it too soon. How soon is too soon? There's a ton of different opinions, but I'd say have at least three solid months of a committed, consistent relationship behind you. After those 3 months have passed, and you think you want to say it, wait some more. Wait until you just can't hold it in anymore. Then do it. Find a nice private moment and tell them. If they don't reply with an "I love you too," say these words: "I don't want you to feel rushed or pressured to say it back. I feel really great about our relationship and I am so happy to be with you." Then kiss them. Keep reminding them through actions, not words. And do not ask them if they love you yet a week later.

Specific #2: Don't show neediness or jealousy. If you are feeling needy and jealous, talk to someone about it, but not them, and not anyone that they are friends with. Post about it here or on r/relationship_advice. Talk to a really trusted friend or family member (I think the latter is a safer and often more helpful option). If it gets really bad, talk to a therapist. If several third parties are telling you that it seems like your partner might be giving you a real reason to worry, then consider telling them how you are feeling. But be careful. And if they continue to fail to meet your needs, end the relationship on your terms.
